verses.note: Paul reads this verse against the risen Christ: the first Adam received life, the last Adam gives it (1 Corinthians 15:45). The resurrection is pictured as a new act of the creator who first breathed life into dust, and Ezekiel's valley of bones uses the same image of breath entering bodies.

The hope that God could give Isaac back from death is not stated in Genesis but drawn from it by Hebrews 11:19, which calls Isaac's return a figure of resurrection. The verse contributes a trust in God's promise that reaches past the point where death seems to end it.

Jesus appeals to the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, all eventually laid in this cave, to argue that God is the God of the living (Matthew 22:31-32). The grave at Machpelah becomes part of the Bible's case for resurrection.

Jesus quotes this verse to answer the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection. God calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob long after their deaths, and Jesus draws the conclusion that he is not the God of the dead but of the living (Mark 12:26-27). The covenant relationship God claims with the patriarchs, long dead when he speaks, implies that death has not ended it.

Peter argues that David died and his tomb was still in Jerusalem, so the words point beyond him to the Messiah whose body did not decay (Acts 2:29-31). The church's confession of the bodily resurrection gives the verse its fullest sense.

The psalm's turn from death's dust to praise, with the answer arriving at the last moment, became for the church the shape of Good Friday turning to Easter. Hebrews 5:7 says Jesus offered prayers with loud cries to the one able to save him from death and was heard.

After being cut off from the land of the living (verse 8) and buried (verse 9), the Servant sees offspring and prolongs his days. The song does not explain how, but it plainly speaks of life beyond his death. The New Testament reads this vindication as fulfilled in Jesus' resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:3-4, according to the Scriptures).

In context the graves are the exile and the resurrection is the return. But the metaphor depends on the conviction that God can raise the dead, and it prepared the way for the explicit hope of Isaiah 26:19 and Daniel 12:2. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.15.1) and Tertullian (On the Resurrection of the Flesh) cited this passage against those who denied the body's resurrection. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 92b) records rabbis debating whether the dead of Ezekiel's valley were actually raised, one sage calling the vision a parable and others insisting it happened.

Matthew narrates the girl's rising with the verb he will use of Jesus' own resurrection. The raising is a return to mortal life, not the resurrection body of the age to come, but it is a sign of that age, and it answers Isaiah's promise, “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise” (Isaiah 26:19).

This is Matthew's first clear prediction of Jesus' resurrection, told in a riddle before the plain predictions of 16:21, 17:23, and 20:19. The one sign given to an unbelieving generation is the Son of Man's return from death, and the chief priests will remember the prediction when they seal the tomb (27:63-64).

Herod's fear shows that the idea of a dead man raised was thinkable in first-century Galilee, though here it is a guilty guess about John, who by John's Gospel did no signs (John 10:41). The chapter lets the reader set this rumor beside the real resurrection Matthew will proclaim, of one who was killed as John was and raised by God.

The only sign Jesus will give his opponents is his own death and resurrection. The verse makes the resurrection not one proof among many but the decisive sign, which Jesus begins to predict openly in verse 21.

From the first prediction, death and resurrection are announced together. The disciples hear only the first half (verse 22), but the resurrection is part of the plan from the start, the sign of Jonah promised in verse 4.

Jesus speaks of his resurrection as certain and uses it as the point from which the transfiguration can be told. The glory seen on the mountain is a preview of the risen Son, and only after Easter can it be understood without being mistaken for the triumph of a political Messiah.

Each prediction ends with the third day. The disciples' grief shows they heard the death more clearly than the rising, but Matthew records the promise so that his readers know the grief was not the last word.
Each prediction ends with the promise of being raised on the third day. The resurrection is part of the plan announced beforehand, not a reversal improvised after the cross.

The stone rejected and then made the cornerstone describes rejection followed by vindication, which the apostles read as the crucifixion and the resurrection (Acts 4:10-11). The reversal is ‘the Lord's doing’, not the builders'.

The riddle only works if resurrection means this life resumed. Jesus will reject that premise, not the resurrection. The case shows how easily the hope of resurrection can be made to look foolish by imagining it too small.

The resurrection is the work of God's power, a new kind of life and not a return to the old. Marriage, bound up in this age with death and the need for heirs, belongs to the present order; the verse says the raised will be like angels in not marrying, not that they become angels or cease to be human.

The hope of resurrection rests on the character of God. Interpreters differ on how the argument works, some seeing it prove that the patriarchs live now with God, which requires a future bodily resurrection to complete their life, others seeing a direct argument that covenant love must defeat death. Both ground the hope in God's faithfulness.

Jesus speaks of his resurrection as certain on the night of his arrest, and he frames it as the restoration of the flock he knows will scatter. The resurrection is not only his vindication but the regathering of the community that failed him.

Matthew places the raising of the saints after Jesus' own raising even though the tombs open at his death. However the timing is read, the point is that Christ is the firstfruits: the general resurrection promised in Ezekiel and Daniel begins with him and because of him (1 Corinthians 15:20-23, Colossians 1:18).

The burial belongs to the gospel Paul received: Christ died, was buried, and was raised (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). A real body in a known tomb, watched by named witnesses, is the ground on which the claim of an empty tomb can be made at all.

Jesus' enemies remember his prediction that he would rise better than his disciples do. Their precaution shows that the resurrection claim was public and specific from the beginning, tied to a known tomb and a named day, and it makes them unwilling witnesses that the tomb was secured.

The angel's words are the first proclamation of the resurrection and hold its essential content: the crucified Jesus is not among the dead, he has been raised, and the place of his body is empty and can be seen. The church confesses the bodily resurrection of the very one who was crucified, not a different, spiritual Jesus.

The women grasp his feet: the risen Jesus has a body that can be held, not a ghost or a vision. Luke and John make the same point in their own ways (Luke 24:39, John 20:27). The resurrection is the raising of the body that was buried.

The story the priests invent assumes the one fact they cannot deny: the body is gone. The earliest recorded explanation offered by the opponents of the resurrection concedes the empty tomb, and the dispute is over why it was empty.
Mark's verb ‘raised’ quietly anticipates later scenes. Jesus raises the sick, raises Jairus's daughter (5:41-42), and is himself raised (16:6).

This is the first raising of the dead in Mark. The girl returns to ordinary mortal life and will die again, so it is a sign rather than the resurrection itself, but Mark describes it with the two verbs he will use for Jesus' own rising, and it points to the one who will conquer death for good.
Feeding the girl proves she is truly alive in the body, as the risen Jesus will later eat before his disciples (Luke 24:41-43). The bodily reality of the raising is part of its meaning.

Most Jews in Jesus' day who hoped for resurrection expected all the righteous to rise together at the end (Daniel 12:2). The disciples' puzzlement is not over the idea of resurrection but over one man, the Son of Man, rising from the dead within history before that day. The verse marks the newness of what Easter would be.

Mark tells the boy's recovery in the words he uses of resurrection, so that the healing becomes a sign of what Jesus will do and what will be done to him. The one who lifts a boy who looked dead will himself be raised.
Every prediction of the passion in Mark ends with the resurrection (8:31, 9:31, 10:34). Jesus' death is never announced as the end; the one who will be killed is the one who will rise.

The psalm turns the parable's ending around. The son killed by the tenants is the stone God sets in the place of honor. Jesus announces not only his rejection but his vindication, and the church read the verse as God's reversal of the cross in the resurrection.

The resurrection is not a resumption of this life's arrangements but a transformation by God's power. Marriage, given for this age, with its task of bearing children in a world of death, is not carried into an age without death. Jesus does not say that the love between people who were married is lost, only that the institution belongs to this age.

Jesus predicts his resurrection before his arrest and makes it the ground of restoring those who will fail him. Resurrection in Mark is not only vindication of Jesus but the reconstitution of his scattered flock.

The Gospel takes care to establish the death: the centurion watched it, confirms it, and Pilate acts on it. The resurrection Mark announces next is not a recovery from a faint but the raising of one who was certainly dead.

The verse joins identity and event: the same Jesus of Nazareth who was crucified has been raised, and the place where his body lay is empty. The church's confession of Christ's bodily resurrection rests on exactly this pairing, the continuity of the person and the reality of the body.

Jesus raises the dead by a direct command in the first person, ‘I tell you, get up’. The young man returns to mortal life and will die again, so this is a sign rather than the resurrection itself, but it shows who holds the power that will raise the dead at the last day (John 5:25-29).

Jesus does not deny the girl's death, which the mourners and the narrator both affirm. He redescribes it: death in his presence is like sleep, from which one wakes. The early church used the same language for believers who die in Christ (1 Thessalonians 4:13-14), and Daniel 12:2 already spoke of those who sleep in the dust awaking.

The girl's return is bodily and ordinary: she stands up and eats. Like the young man at Nain, she will die again, but the story shows Jesus as the Lord of life whose word death obeys, the power that will raise the dead in the end.

From the first prediction, death and resurrection are announced together. The disciples will not understand it (9:45, 18:34), but the resurrection is part of the plan from the beginning, not an afterthought.

The phrase ‘the resurrection of the righteous’ assumes a bodily raising of the dead at the end, when God judges and rewards. It is the only place the Gospels use that exact phrase; Paul, before Felix, speaks of a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked (Acts 24:15), and Daniel 12:2 stands behind both.
The parable ends with the word for resurrection, pointing beyond itself to Easter. The risen Christ will send his disciples back to the Scriptures to understand why he had to rise (24:44-47).
The prediction ends not with death but with rising, and Jesus is its subject. The resurrection is part of the plan announced beforehand, not an unexpected reversal.

The denial of resurrection is the Sadducees' defining mark in Luke-Acts, and the resurrection is the apostles' defining message. This verse introduces the conflict that Jesus' own rising will settle and that Acts will carry on.

The Sadducees' argument works only if resurrection means this life resumed. Jesus' answer will reject that premise, not the resurrection: the age to come is a new mode of life, not an extension of the old arrangements.

The resurrection belongs to the age to come, a different order of existence, and it is received by those God counts worthy. Jesus speaks here of the resurrection of the righteous (compare 14:14), without addressing the resurrection of the wicked that Daniel 12:2 and Acts 24:15 also mention.

The scribes' approval marks the resurrection as common ground between Jesus and the Pharisaic tradition. The argument in Acts over Jesus' resurrection will be not whether God raises the dead but whether he has raised Jesus.

Luke establishes that Jesus was truly dead and buried in a known, unused tomb. The resurrection he proclaims in the next chapter is the raising of this body from this tomb, not a vision detached from the grave, which is why Paul's summary of the gospel includes ‘that He was buried’ (1 Corinthians 15:4).

The risen Jesus has flesh and bones and bears the marks of the cross. The church's confession of the resurrection of the body rests on this continuity: the one who was crucified is raised in the same body, now transformed, not replaced by a spirit.

The resurrection is not added to the suffering as a happy ending; both belong to what is written. Paul's early creed has the same pair and the same reference to Scripture: Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures and was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

Jesus names himself as the one who will raise the destroyed temple. Elsewhere the New Testament usually says that God raised Jesus (Acts 2:24, Romans 10:9), and verse 22 uses the passive; John holds both together, as in 10:17-18, where the Son has authority to lay down his life and take it up again.

The resurrection is what makes sense of the saying. John is candid that the disciples did not understand at the time; their faith was formed by Jesus' rising, which confirmed his word and opened the Scriptures to them (compare Luke 24:44-45).
The Son gives life now (verse 24) and will raise the dead at the end (verses 28-29). The same power operates in both, and it belongs to the Son as it belongs to the Father.

Jesus teaches a general resurrection of the righteous and the wicked, a bodily coming out of tombs at his voice. John does not replace future hope with present experience; he holds both, as the church's creeds confess the resurrection of the dead.

Eternal life begins now for whoever believes (verse 40), yet Jesus still promises resurrection on the last day. John does not let present life replace the future raising of the body; the two belong together.

The fourth and last promise of resurrection in the chapter is attached to eating and drinking. Early writers such as Ignatius (To the Ephesians 20) and Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.18.5, 5.2.3) drew from this link the conviction that bodies nourished by Christ will rise, one reason the church from the start confessed the resurrection of the body and not only the survival of the soul.

Jesus does not deny that believers die bodily; Lazarus will die and be raised (11:25-26). He promises that death will not be the final sight of anyone who keeps his word, because the life he gives is eternal life that death cannot end.

Jesus claims authority to take up his life again. The New Testament usually says that God raised him (Acts 2:24), and here the Son shares that act, one of the places where John shows the Son doing what the Father does (5:21).

Jesus does not correct Martha's belief in a final resurrection; John's Gospel affirms it (5:28-29, 6:40). What he corrects is its distance: the hope she places at the end of history stands before her in person.

The resurrection of the last day is anchored in a person already present. Because life is found in union with Jesus, the believer's future resurrection is certain, and death has lost its power to end the relationship now.

Lazarus returns to ordinary mortal life and will die again, so this is a restoration rather than the resurrection of the last day. The contrast with Jesus' tomb, where the grave clothes are left behind (20:5-7), marks the difference: Jesus rises into a life death can no longer touch (Romans 6:9).

The chief priests, largely Sadducees who denied the resurrection (Acts 23:8), plan to kill a man whose life testifies against their denial. John lets the irony stand: a raised man is dangerous to those whose power depends on death having the last word.
Paul uses the same image of a seed sown and raised for the resurrection body (1 Corinthians 15:36-38). Death is the path to transformed life, first for Jesus and then for those joined to him.

The coming Jesus promises here is first fulfilled on Easter evening, when he came and stood among them (20:19). His resurrection life is the source of theirs: believers live because he lives, the same logic Paul uses when he says our life is hidden with Christ (Colossians 3:3-4).

The labor of the cross ends in the birth of new life. The image suits John's account of Easter, where the disciples' grief becomes joy when they see the Lord (20:20), and Paul's picture of the whole creation groaning in labor pains until the redemption of the body (Romans 8:22-23).

Lazarus came out of his tomb still bound, his face wrapped in a cloth, and had to be set free (11:44); he returned to a life that would end again in death. Jesus leaves the grave clothes behind. The contrast is John's quiet way of saying that this is not resuscitation but resurrection, life that death cannot bind again (Romans 6:9).

The word dei makes the resurrection a necessity of God's purpose, not a surprising accident. The Scriptures, rightly read, required that the Messiah rise, as Jesus tells the disciples on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:25-27, 24:44-46).

The risen Jesus is not bound by locked doors, yet he will show wounds that can be touched (verses 20 and 27). His body is real and continuous with the one that was crucified, and it is also transformed, what Paul calls a spiritual body (1 Corinthians 15:44), not a ghost and not a resuscitated corpse.

The risen body keeps the marks of the cross. Resurrection does not erase the history of suffering; it transfigures it, so that the wounds become the signs by which the Lord is known (Revelation 5:6, the Lamb standing as though slain).

Jesus offers his wounds to be touched. The risen body is tangible, the same body that was crucified, which is why the church has always confessed a bodily resurrection. The text never says Thomas actually touched him; the offer is enough.

The risen Jesus shares a meal with his disciples, as Peter later testifies: they ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead (Acts 10:41). The meal is part of the evidence that his rising was bodily, and it is also a sign of restored fellowship with those who had deserted him.
The resurrection is God's act (‘God raised’) and God's verdict on the one the court condemned. Death's hold on Jesus is described as something that could not last.

The psalm's hope that God would not abandon his faithful one to the grave is read as a promise of bodily resurrection: not escape from death but rescue from its decay. Peter's argument is about the body in the tomb.
The resurrection is presented as an event with witnesses, not as a private experience or a symbol. The apostles' authority in Acts rests on their being witnesses of it (1:22).

The resurrection is the public act by which God installs his Son in power. It is also, by Paul's phrasing, the beginning of the resurrection of the dead: what happened to Jesus is the first fruits of what will happen to his people (1 Corinthians 15:20).
God gives life to the dead: Abraham trusted this about God before the resurrection of Jesus revealed it fully. The same God acted in Isaac's birth from a ‘dead’ body and womb and in raising Jesus.

The resurrection is not an afterthought to justification. It is God's public vindication of the one who died for sinners, and so the declaration that his death has done its work; justification is bound to the risen Christ.

Christ's resurrection is here both the pattern and the power for believers' present life. Paul holds back from saying believers have already been raised (contrast Colossians 2:12 and Ephesians 2:6); in Romans the full share in resurrection is still future (verse 5, 8:11), while its life already shapes how they walk.

Christ ‘cannot die again’: his resurrection is the start of the life of the age to come, not a temporary restoration. That quality of life is what believers are joined to, which is why their hope is secure.

The verse promises the resurrection of believers' bodies, raised by the same God and through the same Spirit who raised Jesus. Christian hope is embodied: God will give life to mortal bodies, not release souls from them.
The final stage of adoption is the body's redemption at the resurrection. Paul's hope for the body is not escape from it but its release from mortality.

The creed places burial between death and raising. That order is why the church has confessed a bodily resurrection: what was raised is what was buried, not a spirit that survived apart from the body.

Paul treats the resurrection as an event with public witnesses who could be questioned, not a private conviction. The Christian claim is historical in form, and the apostle invites scrutiny rather than avoiding it.

The appearance to James is a strong piece of evidence in the historical case for the resurrection: a skeptical brother became a leader of the movement and died for it. Paul does not argue this, but the list places him among those who saw.
Paul will not let Christ's resurrection be treated as a unique exception. The resurrection of Jesus is the first instance of a general resurrection, so to deny the general is to deny the particular.

The resurrection is presented as an act of God: ‘He raised Christ from the dead.’ The New Testament regularly credits the raising to the Father (Acts 2:24, Romans 10:9, Galatians 1:1), and the resurrection is his public vindication of Jesus.

Christ's resurrection is not a private exception but the first part of the one resurrection of the dead. The end-time event Israel hoped for (Daniel 12:2) has begun in the middle of history with one man.

The seed image holds together continuity and change: what is sown is the same thing that grows, and yet what grows is far greater. Death is not an obstacle to resurrection but the condition through which it comes.

The same body is sown and raised, and yet it is raised in a new condition: incorruptible, glorious, powerful. Christian teaching on the resurrection holds both identity (it is this body) and transformation (it is not this body as it is now).

A ‘spiritual body’ is not a spirit instead of a body. The contrast is between the present body, suited to ordinary mortal life, and the resurrection body, wholly suited to and animated by the Spirit of God. The church has rejected readings that make the resurrection body a mere phantom.

Immortality in Paul is not a property the soul already has but a garment God gives at the resurrection. God alone has immortality by nature (1 Timothy 6:16); humans receive it as a gift, and they receive it in the body.

The resurrection is the measure of God's power toward believers. The same power that raised Christ is at work in those who believe, which Ephesians 2:5-6 will apply to their being raised and seated with him.
Christ is the firstborn from the dead, the first to rise into the life of the age to come. The title implies others will follow, as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 15:20-23 with the image of firstfruits.
The resurrection of the dead and eternal judgment belong to the ABCs of the faith, shared ground with Pharisaic Judaism. The letter assumes them as the horizon of everything else (9:27, 11:35).

The contrast between dying priests and the one who ‘lives’ prepares for verse 16. Melchizedek lives only in the sense that Scripture records no death; Jesus lives in fact, by the power of an indestructible life, because he rose.
Jesus holds his priesthood by the power of an indestructible life. The resurrection is not only vindication; it is the ground of his continuing office, since only a living priest can serve ‘forever’.

Premillennial readers take ‘came to life’ as bodily resurrection at Christ's return, the same kind of event as the resurrection of ‘the rest of the dead’ in verse 5, which they place a thousand years later. Either way, the verse insists that those the beast killed are not finally dead.

John 5:24-29 speaks of two ‘hours’: one that ‘now is’, when the spiritually dead hear the Son's voice and live, and one that is coming, when all in the tombs will come out. Amillennial readers find the same two stages here; premillennial readers see two bodily resurrections separated by the millennium. Both read the verse as a promise that death does not have the last word over the faithful.

The verse assumes a general resurrection: those lost at sea, with no grave, and those held by Death and Hades are all restored to stand before God. The church's creeds confess the same, the resurrection of the dead and the judgment of the living and the dead.
